common_name: Gold Medal Rose (Fragrant Deep Golden-Yellow Grandiflora)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Gold Medal is a tall, vigorous 1982 grandiflora valued for deep, saturated yellow color that holds well.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Gold Medal bears large, high-centered, deep golden-yellow double flowers, sometimes edged in a hint of orange-red, with a light fruity fragrance, on a tall, vigorous grandiflora that reaches well over 5 feet. Its rich, saturated yellow color holds better through heat than many older yellow roses, and the tall, upright habit makes it a strong choice for the back of a bed or a low informal screen. As with most classic hybrid tea and grandiflora roses, a regular preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent blooms to sustain repeat flowering, and prune hard in late winter.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tournament of Roses is a 1989 AARS-winning grandiflora named for the annual Pasadena parade.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tournament of Roses bears large, high-centered double flowers in a warm coral-pink blend that darkens toward the petal edges, an All-America Rose Selections winner named for the famous Pasadena New Year's parade. Its vigorous, upright grandiflora habit produces flowers both singly and in small clusters, giving it more versatility for cutting than many pure hybrid teas. A regular preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent blooms to keep the repeat-flowering cycle going, and prune hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: Love Rose (Red and White Bicolor Grandiflora)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Love is a 1980 AARS-winning grandiflora notable for its high-contrast red-and-white bicolor petals.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Love bears high-centered double flowers with bright red petal faces and contrasting white-silver reverses, a striking bicolor combination that was recognized with an All-America Rose Selections award for its distinctiveness in the grandiflora class. Its moderate size and reliable repeat bloom make it a good garden and cutting rose, with the bicolor effect showing best as the outer petals begin to reflex and reveal the pale undersides. A regular preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage rebloom, and prune hard in late winter.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sundowner bears large, high-centered double flowers in warm orange-apricot tones with a strong, spicy-sweet fragrance, an All-America Rose Selections winner bred in Australia and named for the golden colors of sunset it evokes. Its vigorous, upright grandiflora habit and strong scent have kept it popular with gardeners who prioritize fragrance alongside color. A regular preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent blooms to sustain repeat flowering, and prune hard in late winter to encourage strong new growth.

common_name: Pristine Rose (White with Pink Blush Hybrid Tea)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pristine is a 1978 hybrid tea widely regarded as one of the most beautifully formed white roses ever bred.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pristine bears exceptionally large, high-centered, exhibition-quality double blooms in creamy white delicately brushed with pink at the petal edges, widely considered one of the most elegantly formed white-to-pink roses ever introduced. Its refined flower form and light, sweet fragrance have made it a long-standing favorite for exhibition and cutting gardens. As with most classic hybrid teas, a regular preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent blooms to sustain the repeat-flowering cycle, and prune hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth.

common_name: Elle Rose (Soft Pink Blend Hybrid Tea)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Elle is a 2005 AARS-winning hybrid tea bred by Meilland and valued for its soft, romantic coloring and light fragrance.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Elle bears large, high-centered double blooms in a soft blend of pink shading toward yellow at the base, with a light, sweet fragrance, an All-America Rose Selections winner bred by the French Meilland rose house. Its romantic, softly blended color and reliable repeat bloom have made it a popular modern hybrid tea for both garden display and cutting. As with most hybrid teas, a preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, and prune hard in late winter to maintain vigor.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: Rio Samba Rose (Color-Changing Yellow-Orange Hybrid Tea)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Rio Samba is a 1990s hybrid tea whose flowers shift color noticeably from yellow toward orange-pink as they age.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Rio Samba bears high-centered double blooms that open golden-yellow and gradually shift toward orange and pink tones as the flower ages, so a single spray or bush often displays several color stages at once. This lively, ever-changing color effect and reliable repeat bloom have made it a popular choice for gardeners who enjoy variety in the same planting. As with most hybrid teas, a regular preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, and prune hard in late winter to keep the plant vigorous.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: Voodoo Rose (Fragrant Orange-Red Blend Hybrid Tea)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Voodoo is a 1980s hybrid tea known for its warm orange-to-red flame coloring and strong fragrance.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Voodoo bears large, high-centered double blooms opening a warm golden-orange at the base and deepening to a fiery red-orange at the petal edges, with a strong, sweet fragrance that has made it a favorite exhibition and garden hybrid tea since its introduction. Its bold, flame-like color combination stands out clearly against green foliage from a distance. As with most classic hybrid teas, a regular preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent blooms to sustain repeat flowering, and prune hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame
